corrections.reason: Partial indexes and summarising BRIN indexes are documented exceptions.
corrections.original: Every INSERT adds an entry to every index. An UPDATE that changes any indexed column, including `INCLUDE` columns, can't be a **HOT** (heap-only tuple) update, so it adds entries to every index.
corrections.correction: An INSERT maintains applicable indexes; a partial index excludes rows outside its predicate. Changing a column referenced by a non-summarising index, including an `INCLUDE` column, prevents a **HOT** (heap-only tuple) update. BRIN is a summarising-index exception; HOT also requires room on the original heap page.

corrections.reason: Contradicted PostgreSQL 18 skip-scan semantics.
corrections.original: > A range on an early column stops later columns from narrowing the search: in `(ordered_on, customer_id)`, a range on `ordered_on` means `customer_id` can only be checked entry by entry.
corrections.correction: > Equality on leading keys and a range on the next key establish the usual scan bounds. Later conditions can still be checked within the index, and PostgreSQL 18 skip scan may perform additional searches to narrow work further. Check the actual plan rather than treating the rule as absolute.

1. Index entries don't record transaction visibility; the heap does.
2. The visibility map has a bit per heap page: "every row here is visible to everyone".

corrections.original:
How a HOT update works:

1. If no indexed column changes and the page has free space, the new row version goes on the same page, chained from the old one.
2. Indexes still point to the old version and follow the chain. No index writes.

Once `total` is in an index (even as INCLUDE), changing it means:

1. Not HOT-eligible.
2. New entries in applicable ordinary indexes, plus more WAL; partial indexes omit nonmatching rows and summarising indexes such as BRIN behave differently.

Check `n_tup_hot_upd` vs `n_tup_upd` in `pg_stat_user_tables` before and after. Only cover columns that rarely change.
